prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Sen. Hillary Clinton's chief presidential campaign strategist is quitting his post amid criticism of his public relations firm's contacts with the Colombian government over a pending free-trade deal, Clinton's campaign announced. Mark Penn will continue to advise Hillary Clinton's presidential campaign. Mark Penn and his political consulting firm will continue to advise the New York senator's Democratic presidential bid, but Penn will give up his job as chief strategist, campaign manager Maggie Williams said. "After the events of the last few days, Mark Penn has asked to give up his role as chief strategist of the Clinton campaign," Williams said. Clinton did not answer reporters' questions about Penn's exit during a campaign stop in New Mexico on Sunday. Penn is CEO of public relations giant Burson-Marsteller and is president of Penn, Schoen and Berland, his political consulting firm. Friday, he acknowledged he had met with the Colombian ambassador to the United States earlier in the week in his role as Burson-Marsteller's chief to discuss the pending U.S.-Colombia trade pact, which Clinton has criticized on the campaign trail. Penn called the meeting "an error in judgment that will not be repeated," and apologized. That prompted Colombia's government to fire the company Saturday, calling the remarks "a lack of respect to Colombians." Clinton and top aides were sharply critical of rival Democrat Barack Obama in February when reports indicated that his top economic adviser had suggested to a Canadian official that Obama was not as supportive of changes to the North American Free Trade Agreement as the Illinois senator claimed to be on the campaign trail. Penn said Friday that Clinton's opposition to the U.S.-Colombia pact, which the Bush administration is trying to push through Congress, "is clear and was not discussed" during his meeting with the ambassador. And Clinton spokesman Mo Elleithee said Penn's meeting was "not in any way done on behalf of the campaign." But Pennsylvania Gov. Ed Rendell -- a key Clinton backer in his state's April 22 primary -- suggested Sunday that Penn needed to go. "I think you've got to make it very clear for someone who is a consultant, who you are representing and who you are not representing, and I would hope that Mr. Penn, when he talked to the Colombians, made that clear. And it doesn't sound to me like he did, and that's something the campaign should take into question," Rendell told NBC's "Meet the Press." Sources in the Clinton campaign said that Penn realized this weekend that he needed to step aside, and that Clinton was disappointed that he had met with the Colombians. E-mail to a friend .

**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** Sen. Hillary Clinton’s chief presidential campaign strategist is stepping down from his post amid criticism over his public relations firm’s contacts with the Colombian government regarding a pending free-trade agreement, Clinton’s campaign announced.

Mark Penn and his political consulting firm will continue to advise the New York senator’s Democratic presidential campaign, but Penn will relinquish his role as chief strategist, campaign manager Maggie Williams said.

“After the events of the last few days, Mark Penn has asked to give up his role as chief strategist of the Clinton campaign,” Williams said.

Clinton did not respond to reporters’ questions about Penn’s departure during a campaign stop in New Mexico on Sunday.

Penn is CEO of public relations giant Burson-Marsteller and president of Penn, Schoen and Berland, his political consulting firm. On Friday, he acknowledged that, in his capacity as head of Burson-Marsteller, he had met earlier in the week with the Colombian ambassador to the United States to discuss the pending U.S.-Colombia trade pact, which Clinton has criticized on the campaign trail.

Penn called the meeting “an error in judgment that will not be repeated” and apologized. In response, the Colombian government fired the company on Saturday, calling his remarks “a lack of respect to Colombians.”

In February, Clinton and her top aides sharply criticized Democratic rival Barack Obama after reports indicated that his chief economic adviser had suggested to a Canadian official that Obama was less supportive of changes to the North American Free Trade Agreement than the Illinois senator had claimed on the campaign trail.

Penn said Friday that Clinton’s opposition to the U.S.-Colombia pact, which the Bush administration is seeking to push through Congress, “is clear and was not discussed” during his meeting with the ambassador. Clinton spokesman Mo Elleithee also said Penn’s meeting was “not in any way done on behalf of the campaign.”

However, Pennsylvania Gov. Ed Rendell—a key Clinton supporter ahead of his state’s April 22 primary—suggested Sunday that Penn needed to step down.

“I think you’ve got to make it very clear for someone who is a consultant, who you are representing and who you are not representing, and I would hope that Mr. Penn, when he talked to the Colombians, made that clear. And it doesn’t sound to me like he did, and that’s something the campaign should take into question,” Rendell told NBC’s *Meet the Press*.

Sources within the Clinton campaign said Penn realized over the weekend that he needed to step aside and that Clinton was disappointed he had met with the Colombians.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign announced that Sen. Clinton’s top strategist, Mark Penn, is stepping down from that position following controversy over his public relations company’s dealings with the Colombian government regarding a proposed free-trade agreement.

Penn and his political consulting firm will remain advisers to the New York senator’s Democratic presidential campaign, but he will no longer serve as chief strategist, according to campaign manager Maggie Williams.

“In light of what has occurred over the past several days, Mark Penn has requested that he relinquish his position as the Clinton campaign’s chief strategist,” Williams said.

During a Sunday campaign appearance in New Mexico, Clinton did not respond to reporters’ questions about Penn’s departure from the role.

Penn is the chief executive of the major public relations firm Burson-Marsteller. He also heads his political consulting company, Penn, Schoen and Berland.

On Friday, Penn confirmed that, while acting in his Burson-Marsteller capacity, he had met earlier in the week with Colombia’s ambassador to the United States. Their discussion concerned the proposed U.S.-Colombia trade agreement, which Clinton has opposed while campaigning.

Penn apologized and described the meeting as “an error in judgment that will not be repeated.” The Colombian government responded Saturday by dismissing Burson-Marsteller, saying Penn’s comments demonstrated “a lack of respect to Colombians.”

In February, Clinton and senior members of her campaign had strongly criticized Democratic opponent Barack Obama after reports said his chief economic adviser had indicated to a Canadian official that Obama was less committed to revising the North American Free Trade Agreement than his campaign statements suggested. Obama was then an Illinois senator.

Penn said Friday that Clinton’s position against the U.S.-Colombia agreement—which the Bush administration was seeking to move through Congress—“is clear and was not discussed” in his conversation with the ambassador. Clinton spokesman Mo Elleithee also said the meeting was “not in any way done on behalf of the campaign.”

However, Pennsylvania Gov. Ed Rendell, an important Clinton supporter ahead of the state’s April 22 primary, indicated Sunday that Penn should leave his role.

Rendell told NBC’s “Meet the Press” that consultants must clearly identify whom they do and do not represent. He said he hoped Penn had explained that distinction to the Colombian officials, but added that it did not appear Penn had done so and that the campaign should examine the matter.

Clinton campaign sources said Penn concluded over the weekend that he should step aside. They also said Clinton was disappointed that he had held the meeting with Colombian representatives.

counterfactuals.output:
# Penn steps down as Clinton campaign’s chief strategist

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Mark Penn stepped down Sunday as chief strategist for Sen. Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign following controversy over his contacts with the Colombian government concerning a proposed free-trade agreement.

Penn, who also led the public relations firm Burson-Marsteller, met with Colombia’s ambassador to the United States to discuss the trade deal. The meeting drew criticism because Clinton had publicly opposed the agreement while campaigning for the Democratic presidential nomination.

“After the events of the last few days, Mark Penn has asked to give up his role as chief strategist of the Clinton campaign,” campaign manager Maggie Williams said in a statement.

Penn and his polling firm, Penn, Schoen & Berland Associates, will continue to provide polling and advice to the campaign, Williams said.

Penn described the meeting with Colombian Ambassador Carolina Barco as an “error in judgment” and said it had not been conducted on behalf of the Clinton campaign. Burson-Marsteller had been working for Colombia to promote congressional approval of the trade pact.

The Colombian government subsequently ended its relationship with the firm, saying Penn’s comments showed a lack of respect toward the country.

The controversy came at a sensitive time for Clinton, who was locked in a closely contested primary campaign against Sen. Barack Obama. Clinton had emphasized her opposition to the Colombia agreement, arguing that labor and human-rights concerns needed to be addressed before it could move forward.

Penn had been one of Clinton’s most influential advisers and helped shape the campaign’s strategy and message. His departure from the top strategic role represented another shake-up for the campaign as it prepared for the Pennsylvania primary and the remaining Democratic contests.
